analysis.one_liner: Permanently bans offshore oil and gas drilling off the California, Oregon, and Washington coasts.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 39 House Democrats, has sat in the House Natural Resources Committee with no hearing or vote since April 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes a permanent ban into law against any new federal leasing or drilling for oil and gas in federal waters off the Pacific coast, from Washington through Southern California. Today the coast is protected mainly by federal leasing plans, which can change with each administration; this would make the protection permanent in statute. It went to the House Natural Resources Committee in April 2025 and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal communities whose economies depend on fishing, tourism, and clean beaches, plus anyone who values keeping the Pacific coast free of new drilling infrastructure and the spill risk that comes with it.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so that the Interior Secretary may not issue any lease or authorization for oil or gas exploration, development, or production in the Washington/Oregon, Northern California, Central California, and Southern California planning areas.
The prohibition is written to apply notwithstanding any other provision of law, meaning a future administration could not simply reverse it through a new leasing program as it could current policy.
The ban covers the entire West Coast planning area as defined in the 2024-2029 federal offshore leasing program, locking in the coast's current drilling-free status permanently.

analysis.who_pays: The oil and gas industry, which forgoes permanent access to federal waters off the West Coast for exploration and drilling. Critics also argue the country gives up a potential future energy supply.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently removes a large federal offshore area from potential energy development, which opponents argue limits domestic oil and gas supply and could raise costs or reduce energy security over the long term.

The West Coast currently has no active offshore drilling leases and the 2024-2029 leasing program already excludes new West Coast sales, so the bill's practical effect is to make existing policy permanent rather than to change conditions on the water today; critics can call that redundant legislation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who live on or visit the Pacific coast, the benefit is permanent protection against new drilling and the spill risk that comes with it, at no direct cost to them. The cost falls on an industry that has no current leases or leases pending in these waters anyway, though energy-security arguments in favor of keeping areas open are a legitimate objection. The bill is straightforward in design; its weakness is political, not substantive.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on April 10, 2025, referred to the House Natural Resources Committee, and has taken no further step in the record since then.

narrative.text: Representative Jared Huffman introduced the bill on April 10, 2025, joined by 25 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day.
It has attracted 39 Democratic cosponsors but no Republicans, and no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled in the record since its referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo holds: the West Coast stays off the leasing map under current federal policy, and the oil and gas industry faces no new restrictions, while coastal protection advocates have not gained the permanent ban they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no permanent ban yet

for.name: Jared Huffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to permanently ban West Coast offshore oil and gas drilling.

for.name: 39 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor listed is a Democrat.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred to the committee on April 10, 2025; no hearing or markup appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: All 39 cosponsors are House Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican in a Republican-controlled House; no Republican supports it in the record.

industries.note: The bill permanently closes federal waters off Washington, Oregon, and California to new oil and gas leasing and drilling. The industry profits by extracting in these waters, while the spill and industrialization risk falls on coastal communities, so the bill directly takes away future access.

industries.industry: Pacific coast fishing, tourism, and recreation businesses
industries.note: A permanent drilling ban protects the clean coastline, fishing grounds, and beaches these businesses depend on. Their interest runs alongside the public's.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no hearing, and no committee action since April 2025 in a House controlled by the opposing party, the bill is very unlikely to receive a vote this Congress. Similar West Coast drilling bans have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses without becoming law. Its main value is establishing positions and building cosponsor support for future sessions.
